lead: A system kept at constant temperature and volume, or at constant temperature and pressure, is judged not by U or H alone but by two combinations: the Helmholtz function A = U − TS and the Gibbs function G = H − TS. Their fall tells which way a process can go on its own and how much work can be taken out. Chemists use G to decide whether a reaction runs; engineers use it for phase change, equilibrium and fuel cells. This chapter defines both functions, finds their differentials, and reads the two tests for spontaneous change from them.
prereq: You need: Exact differentials, reciprocity and cyclic relations, the relation T dS = dU + p dV, and the entropy principle.

blocks.text: The natural variables of U are entropy and volume, and no laboratory controls entropy. Two combinations replace entropy by temperature.

Helmholtz function: A = U − TS, also written F and called the Helmholtz free energy. Gibbs function: G = H − TS, the Gibbs free energy, with H = U + pV. U, H, TS, A and G are all in kJ when T is in K and S in kJ/K. Per kg, a = u − Ts and g = h − Ts are in kJ/kg.
A = U − TS          G = H − TS
blocks.where: U is internal energy, H enthalpy (kJ); T is absolute temperature (K); S is entropy (kJ/K). Both A and G are built only from properties, so they are properties too, and their changes depend only on the end states.

blocks.text: Start from dU = T dS − p dV for a closed system that does only pV work.

items: Differentiate A = U − TS: dA = dU − T dS − S dT. The T dS inside dU cancels the −T dS, leaving dA = −S dT − p dV, so A is naturally a function of T and V.
Differentiate G = H − TS with dH = T dS + V dp: dG = dH − T dS − S dT = −S dT + V dp, so G is naturally a function of T and p.

blocks.text: In both new differentials the coefficient of dT is −S: (∂G/∂T)p = −S, so G falls as T rises, faster for the phase with more entropy. Figure 4.4.1 uses this slope for ice and water. These four differentials are exact, and their cross-derivatives give the Maxwell relations.

sections.h3: What the fall of A and G means

items: A closed system at temperature T exchanges heat Q with surroundings at the same T. First law: Q = ΔU + W, where W is the work done by the system.
Entropy principle for system and surroundings: ΔS − Q/T ≥ 0, so Q ≤ TΔS.
Put this in the first law: W ≤ TΔS − ΔU = −ΔA. The work from a process at constant T cannot exceed the fall of A.
At constant T and V with no other work, W = 0, so ΔA ≤ 0: A falls until it reaches a minimum, which is equilibrium.
At constant T and p split W into pV work pΔV and useful work W<sub>u</sub>: then W<sub>u</sub> ≤ −ΔG. With no useful work, ΔG ≤ 0, and equilibrium is the minimum of G.

blocks.text: So −ΔA is the largest total work at constant T, and −ΔG is the largest non-pV (electrical or chemical) work at constant T and p. A battery or a fuel cell delivers at most −ΔG of electrical work. A turbine is a different case: its shaft work is limited by the fall in flow exergy, not by −ΔG.

For a pure substance the Gibbs function per mole is the chemical potential. Two phases of a pure substance are in equilibrium when their specific Gibbs functions are equal, gliquid = gsolid: this is the starting point of the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.

examples.question: 1 kg of air (ideal gas, R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K)) is compressed slowly and isothermally at 300 K from 100 kPa to 500 kPa. Find ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔA and ΔG, and the least work needed.
steps: Ideal gas at constant T: ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0, because u and h depend on T only.
Gibbs: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = 0 + 138.6 = +138.6 kJ, equal to ΔA because Δ(pV) = mRΔT = 0.
Work: at constant T, W ≤ −ΔA = −138.6 kJ, so at least 138.6 kJ must be done on the gas. Check: reversible isothermal work = mRT·ln(p₂/p₁) = 0.287 × 300 × 1.6094 = 138.6 kJ.
examples.answer: ΔU = ΔH = 0; ΔS = −0.4619 kJ/K; ΔA = ΔG = +138.6 kJ; the least work input is 138.6 kJ.

examples.question: Water freezes at 273.15 K and 1 atm with latent heat 333.5 kJ/kg. Taking Δh and Δs of freezing as constant over ±10 K, find Δg for freezing 1 kg at 273.15 K, at 263.15 K and at 283.15 K, and say what each result means. Also find Δa at 273.15 K, with v = 0.0010002 m³/kg for water and 0.0010908 m³/kg for ice.
steps: Freezing releases heat: Δh = −333.5 kJ/kg. At the normal freezing point, Δs = Δh/T = −333.5/273.15 = −1.2209 kJ/(kg·K).
At 273.15 K: Δg = Δh − TΔs = −333.5 + 273.15 × 1.2209 = −333.5 + 333.5 = 0. Ice and water are in equilibrium.
At 263.15 K (supercooled water): Δg = −333.5 + 263.15 × 1.2209 = −333.5 + 321.3 = −12.2 kJ/kg. Negative, so freezing goes on its own.
At 283.15 K: Δg = −333.5 + 283.15 × 1.2209 = −333.5 + 345.7 = +12.2 kJ/kg. Positive, so water cannot freeze; ice melts instead.
Δa at 273.15 K: at constant T and p, Δa = Δg − pΔv. Δv = 0.0010908 − 0.0010002 = 9.06 × 10⁻⁵ m³/kg (ice takes more room), so Δa = 0 − 101.325 × 9.06 × 10⁻⁵ = −0.0092 kJ/kg.
examples.answer: Δg = 0 at 273.15 K (equilibrium), −12.2 kJ/kg at 263.15 K (water freezes) and +12.2 kJ/kg at 283.15 K (ice melts). Δa at the freezing point is −0.0092 kJ/kg: small, but not zero.

traps: Sign slip: dA = −S dT − p dV but dG = −S dT + V dp. The second term changes both sign and variable.
Using ΔG ≤ 0 as the test at constant T and V. There the test is ΔA ≤ 0, with equilibrium at the minimum of A.
Units: A and G are in kJ; a = u − Ts and g = h − Ts are in kJ/kg, with u and h in kJ/kg and only s in kJ/(kg·K).
Reading ΔG = 0 as "nothing can happen". It means the two states are in equilibrium, like ice and water at 273.15 K.

quiz.q: Define the Helmholtz and Gibbs functions and give their units.
quiz.a: A = U − TS and G = H − TS, both in kJ (per kg: a = u − Ts and g = h − Ts in kJ/kg).

quiz.q: Name the natural variables of A and of G.
quiz.a: A: T and V. G: T and p.

quiz.q: Why does the T dS term cancel when dA is formed?
quiz.a: dU = T dS − p dV already carries +T dS, and d(TS) = T dS + S dT. Subtracting leaves dA = −S dT − p dV, so A depends naturally on T and V.

quiz.q: At 300 K and 1 atm a process has ΔH = −50 kJ and ΔS = −0.1 kJ/K. Find ΔG and say whether it can go on its own.
quiz.a: ΔG = −50 − 300 × (−0.1) = −50 + 30 = −20 kJ. Negative, so it can go on its own at constant T and p.

quiz.q: A closed system at constant temperature has ΔA = −120 kJ. What is the most work it can deliver?
A student says a state at constant T and V is at equilibrium because ΔG = 0. What is wrong?
quiz.a: The Gibbs test belongs to constant T and p. At constant T and V the test is the Helmholtz function: equilibrium is the minimum of A, with ΔA ≤ 0 for any possible change.

quiz.q: A fuel reaction has ΔG = −40 kJ at 298 K, yet a mixture of the reactants sits unchanged for years. Explain.
quiz.a: ΔG gives the driving force, not the speed. A high activation barrier keeps the reaction slow; thermodynamics says it can go, kinetics says how fast.

beyond: Phase-diagram software such as Thermo-Calc stores the Gibbs function of each phase as a function of temperature, pressure and composition, and finds the stable phases by minimising the total G (the CALPHAD method). Fuel-cell designers use −ΔG of the cell reaction to set the ideal cell voltage. Search next: CALPHAD, Gibbs energy minimisation, reversible cell voltage.

figure.caption: The Gibbs function of ice and of liquid water against temperature: the lines cross at 273.15 K, where freezing has Δg = 0. Ten kelvin either side the gap is 12.2 kJ/kg, and the phase with the lower g is the one that forms. The slopes are drawn only roughly; the gaps carry the numbers.

spec.aria: Two falling straight lines, ice and liquid water, crossing at 273.15 K. Water falls more steeply. At 263.15 K ice is 12.2 kJ/kg lower, so water freezes; at 283.15 K water is 12.2 kJ/kg lower, so ice melts.
